title: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Education Teaching on Purpose 4
author: Kohlbeck, Adam
summary: Kohlbeck, in conversation with practitioner-leader Yamina Bibi, examines how whole-school routines for securing and regaining student attention work -- and why they sometimes fail. The case for school-wide attention cues (such as 3-2-1 SLANT) rests less on any particular method and more on the consistency and shared belief that make any routine function. The article distinguishes between whole-class calls for attention, which benefit from uniformity, and micro-interventions for individual off-task students, where minimally invasive techniques are more appropriate. Mandated whole-school routines succeed based on implementation: teachers who understand the problem the routine is solving and believe in the underlying logic use it with conviction. Kohlbeck draws on Amjad Ali's framework -- communicate the data, the problem, the collective action, and the anticipated reward -- before introducing any whole-school mandate. The broader insight is that teacher agency and whole-school practice are not opposites; the tension dissolves when the conversation about context and purpose has genuinely happened.
points: - The most important variable is not which attention cue a school uses but whether every teacher believes in the expectation behind it -- compliance without conviction produces routines that fade rather than stick. - Whole-school attention calls benefit from predictability as students move between classrooms; a consistent signal reduces cognitive load and builds the familiarity that makes transitions smoother. - Minimally invasive techniques (hand on desk, walking toward off-task students) serve a different purpose from whole-class signals -- using a whole-school call to redirect two students would unnecessarily disrupt the rest. - Before mandating any school-wide approach, leaders should follow Ali's four-step framing: share the data, name the problem, describe the collective action, articulate the reward that will be felt collectively. - Teacher agency and standardised routines are not inherently in conflict; the tension dissolves when the why is clear and professionals have had genuine input into the diagnosis, even if not into the specific solution.
quotes: Whether you prefer more or less precision around a call for attention is not the important thing. The important thing is that you are working in a school in which you have belief in the expectation.

If every teacher is using 3,2,1 SLANT as their call for attention then this creates an element of predictability and familiarity for students as they move from one teacher to the next. Everyone knows what is expected and how to meet those expectations.

In that instance, they probably would not use a whole class call for attention even though securing attention is the purpose they are trying to serve. Instead, they may use a minimally invasive technique like a hand on the desk or simply walking over to the students in order to regain their attention specifically.
People tend to be quite happy with a whole school call for attention if there has been proper consultation around it and if they understand the problem they are trying to solve.

With teacher agency rightly high on the national agenda, we must be careful to not assume that any attempt to establish shared routines in a school is automatically a bad thing. The answer to when should you implement a whole school shared approach is usually it depends, and a conversation about context is required.

Student attention is an ongoing challenge. With so many potential distractions in even the most well thought out classrooms, teachers have a consistent, if not constant, challenge to keep attention where they need it to be.
